acts.title: The vandalism problem, in one meeting
text: This is the second time this month that we have had a ___ problem at the factory.
Cameras are the obvious answer, but they are expensive to install and difficult to ___ .
For a small business that makes them too ___ to consider seriously.
So I do not think cameras are an ___ , I am afraid.
Lights that come on when they sense movement would cost far less, and anti-climb paint on the wall would be a sensible extra ___ .

items.q: Security cameras are expensive to ___.

tts: Mike, what are we going to do about this vandalism problem at the factory? It is the second time this month. First graffiti, now broken windows.
I know. It is obviously bored kids with nothing better to do. They are clearly not interested in stealing anything.
I have had enough of it. One alternative would be to install some security cameras.

That would be the obvious solution, but we need to take cost into consideration. Security cameras are expensive to set up and difficult to maintain. We are a small business. So I do not think that is an option, I am afraid.
Would it be worth putting in some of those fake cameras — the ones that look real but are not?

I am not convinced by those, to be honest, and I do not think the vandals are either. I think a better way forward would be to put in some of those lights that come on only when they sense movement. Vandals are less likely to commit crimes in well-lit areas.

Do you think there would be any point in changing the lock on the gate? — No, the lock has not been broken. They have climbed over the wall. — In that case, what if we also paint the walls with anti-climb paint, just as a precaution? — There is no harm in doing that as well.

acts.title: Boredom
tts: Like many people I spend most of my day rushing around — answering the phone, responding to emails, attending meeting after meeting. I never seem to stop doing things. So whenever I can, I grab a book, find a quiet spot and relax. But then, after a while, I get bored, and I swap my book for my phone.

How can we be busier than ever before and still feel bored? The first answer is that while we may feel a lot busier, statistics show that we actually work a lot less than we used to. In Germany people work forty-one per cent fewer hours than they did in 1950. In the Netherlands, forty per cent fewer; in the UK, twenty-four point six per cent fewer.

One reason we feel busier is that the boundaries between our home life and our work life are blurred. In 1950 most people worked in workplaces, so when they were at work they worked and when they were at home they did not. Today many of us end up working at home in the evenings.

The modern concept of boredom is relatively recent. The word first appeared in the Charles Dickens novel Bleak House in 1852. Before the nineteenth century most jobs were physically demanding; the Industrial Revolution created factories and production lines, and those jobs were very repetitive and, as a result, boring.

Today, thanks to faster internet speeds, we have access to instant entertainment wherever we are. But does this mean the end of boredom? No. Many experts say we are more easily bored than ever, because the minute we become bored with something we can change it.

items.q: What is the apparent contradiction the video explores?
o: We work less than we used to but feel busier and get bored faster
People work longer hours than ever

items.q: Why do people feel busier, according to the video?
o: The boundary between home and work has blurred

items.q: When did the word “boredom” first appear?
Why are we more easily bored now?
o: Because we can change what we are doing the moment it bores us

acts.title: Boredom
tts: In Germany people work forty-one per cent fewer hours than they did in 1950. In the UK the figure is twenty-four point six per cent fewer. Even in the USA, where working hours are generally longer than in Europe, the average employee spends ten per cent less time working than sixty-five years ago.
The word boredom first appeared in the Charles Dickens novel Bleak House in 1852. Over the last hundred and sixty-five years it has become a popular way to describe tedious situations.
The Industrial Revolution created factories and production lines. These jobs were very repetitive and, as a result, boring.

This culture of instant gratification has resulted in shorter attention spans, and as a result we quickly become restless. Perhaps we need to forget about doing lots of things at once and focus on one thing — like a book.

acts.title: Proposing a solution, and saying why it will not work
rule: Solving a problem in English follows a shape: propose, evaluate, reject or accept. Almost every phrase in the set is built on either would be to + infinitive or a preposition followed by an -ing form, which is why this lesson recycles Lesson 34 rather than introducing anything new.
points: One alternative would be to… / A better way forward would be to… Both take an infinitive.
Would it be worth …-ing? / Is there any point in …-ing? Both take -ing, because worth and in are followed by the -ing form.
I don’t think that’s an option, I’m afraid. / I’m not convinced by that, to be honest.
We need to take cost into consideration. The fixed phrase is take something into consideration.
There’s no harm in …-ing. Again, -ing after in.
What if we…? followed by a present or past form: what if we paint / what if we painted.
eg: One alternative would be to install cameras.
Proposal, infinitive.
A better way forward would be to put in lights.
Proposal, infinitive.
Would it be worth putting in fake ones?
worth + -ing.
Is there any point in changing the lock?
in + -ing.
We need to take cost into consideration.
Fixed phrase.
I don’t think that’s an option, I’m afraid.
Gentle rejection.
I’m not convinced by that, to be honest.
Gentle rejection, stronger.
There’s no harm in doing that as well.
in + -ing.
What if we painted the walls too?
Informal suggestion.
That would be an effective solution.
Acceptance.
acts.careful: “Would it be worth to put in cameras” and “any point to change the lock” are both wrong. worth and in are followed by an -ing form, every time.

write.q: Write an article of about 200 words giving advice on a real problem — at your workplace, in your building, in your town. State the problem, give two possible solutions with their drawbacks, and recommend one. Use at least three proposing phrases from this lesson, and check that every one is followed by the right form.
write.model:
The problem in our courtyard is not parking. It is that six of the twenty spaces are occupied by cars that have not moved since 2021.

One alternative would be to have them towed, which is what everybody suggests within about four minutes of any conversation on the subject. We need to take the law into consideration, though: the cars are on private land, none of them is a danger, and removing somebody’s property costs the building more in legal fees than the spaces are worth.

A second alternative would be to introduce paid parking. Would it be worth charging a small monthly amount for a numbered space? It would certainly move the dead cars. It would also mean the two households who genuinely cannot pay would lose a space they have had for fifteen years, which I am not willing to propose.

A better way forward would be to write to the six owners, individually and by post, giving three months. There is no harm in trying it first, it costs the price of six stamps, and my guess is that four of the six cars would go.
